packets.key_finding: A nudge that shrouds the minimum-payment autopay default cut exact-minimum-payment behavior by 23% over six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because liquidity-constrained cardholders simply chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit cards, six-month follow-up, National Bureau of Economic Research working paper.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry: a choice-architecture change can shift nominal enrollment/behavior sharply while leaving the real outcome (debt/savings) unchanged, which is exactly the enrollment-vs-amount distinction the brief asks us to test before defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings accumulation
shrouding a payment option differs structurally from opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer financial field experiment showing a default/nudge changes surface behavior without changing the underlying financial outcome, the core 'vanity metric' concern in the brief.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but implementing a default -- especially one the client then refuses -- significantly lowered how trustworthy and honest the advice was perceived to be.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European experiment, on financial default framing in wealth management.
packets.why_it_matters: Empirically shows the exact reputational trade-off the brief flags: a default that moves behavior can simultaneously read as manipulative and damage perceived trust, which should directly weigh against opt-out and toward active-choice or careful framing for entry design.
limitations: wealth-management advice context, not a mobile round-up feature
risk-taking allocation decisions, not enrollment/withdrawal from a savings pot
packets.relevance_reason: Directly tests when a financial default is perceived as manipulative in a European consumer setting, the manipulation-risk question the brief asks about.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Accounting for job turnover, vesting, and opt-outs, automatic enrollment raises steady-state savings by only 0.6% of income and auto-escalation by 0.3%, with only 40% of employees escalating on their first scheduled date.
packets.methodology: Analysis of administrative data from nine 401(k) plans incorporating medium- and long-run dynamics (turnover, withdrawal, opt-out).
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative statement of the support team's objection: once you follow people past enrollment, automatic-default effects on real savings amounts are much smaller than the headline enrollment-rate lift suggests.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated auto-escalation differs from a self-set multiplier
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with quantified medium/long-run attenuation, exactly the evidence the brief asked us to find.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when default effects persist, fade, or reverse downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: Theoretical synthesis and taxonomy-building across the consumer-default literature. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete list of moderators (antecedent preferences, trade-off salience, time course) the team should measure when evaluating whether round-up enrollment defaults persist past sign-up -- directly shapes what the 6-12 month follow-up study should track.
limitations: conceptual framework, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: General-purpose consumer psychology framework for exactly the downstream persistence/disengagement question the brief raises.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: In 8.6 million tipping decisions, 84% of default adherence arose from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out effort cost together (friction complementarity); adding a lower option (15%) below an existing 20-25-30% menu captured 69% of achievable consumer welfare gains at only 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural model estimated on 8.6 million real transactions plus an independent stated-preference survey of preferences.
packets.why_it_matters: The counterfactual on adding a lower preset option is a direct, quantified answer to the multiplier-menu question: it shows how much welfare is left on the table by a restrictive menu and how cheaply it can be recovered, a method that transfers straightforwardly to designing the 1x/2x/5x round-up menu.
limitations: taxi tipping, not a savings product
monetary stakes and decision frequency differ substantially from a savings sweep
packets.relevance_reason: Named method transfer: a structural default-menu model decomposing deviation cost and opt-out cost, plus a counterfactual on adding a lower preset tier, applies directly to designing the round-up multiplier menu.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Maps EU law on dark patterns and offers a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from manipulation warranting regulation.
packets.methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only, no empirical data.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal test for when a pre-selected opt-out default crosses from helpful nudge into a regulated dark pattern, which should directly shape whether we choose opt-out, opt-in, or active choice and how we disclose the exit.
limitations: normative/legal framework, not an empirical measure of enrolment or behavior change
not specific to financial products or round-up savings
packets.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's stated reputational risk that an opt-out default could read as a dark pattern in the EU regulatory context.
packets.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
packets.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still held both defaults after three years.
packets.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms.
packets.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set contribution level anchors most participants for years, directly warning that whichever multiplier (1x/2x/5x) is pre-selected in the round-up feature is likely to become the de facto ceiling for most users.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, not a consumer app
no publication year given, indicating this is the classic study current literature argues with
packets.relevance_reason: The classic result on anchoring at a pre-set contribution level, the direct precedent for the multiplier pre-selection decision.
packets.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive to the value of the default option, even when it causes substantial losses.
packets.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options in a large administrative claims setting.
packets.why_it_matters: Strong causal evidence that default persistence can reflect true inattention rather than considered choice -- a caution against assuming opt-out enrollment reflects genuine preference, relevant to the manipulation-risk question.
limitations: government health-insurance enrollment, not a consumer fintech product
no employer-style trusted intermediary but also no app/liquidity context
packets.relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on default persistence and insensitivity to value, informing how much weight to put on opt-out enrollment numbers.
packets.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
packets.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

packets.key_finding: Two field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision) increases desired behavior versus no intervention, and a refined 'enhanced active choice' that frames losses in the non-preferred option performs even better, recommended as a complement to or substitute for automatic enrollment.
packets.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments comparing active choice, enhanced active choice, and no-default conditions.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, tested alternative to full opt-out enrolment — forced active choice with loss-framed messaging — that could capture much of the enrolment lift without passively sweeping in disengaged users, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: field experiments are in health/medication and general savings contexts, not a mobile banking round-up feature
no 6-12 month persistence data reported in the abstract
enhanced active choice framing itself risks reading as manipulative under EU dark-pattern scrutiny
packets.relevance_reason: The core paper testing whether active choice (and an enhanced variant) gets most of the default's benefit, which is exactly the brief's stated open question.
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

packets.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrolment raised participation to over 85%, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and default fund, and half still did so after three years, roughly offsetting the participation gain against a lower savings rate per person.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking automatic-enrolment participants for up to three years.
packets.why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a low preset default anchors contribution levels for years, directly warning against shipping a low pre-selected round-up multiplier if the goal is meaningful savings amounts rather than nominal enrolment.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan, not a self-directed consumer app
over two decades old, predating the app/liquidity/regulatory context the brief flags as changed
does not measure withdrawal or disengagement, only contribution-rate anchoring
packets.relevance_reason: Foundational evidence on anchoring at a preset default level, the exact mechanism the brief worries about for the round-up multiplier decision.
packets.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: With a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had opted out by 12 months (versus roughly half in plans with lower defaults), and many who stayed at the default had incomes suggesting 12% was a poor fit, with low-income employees anchoring most strongly.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from an employer retirement plan; longitudinal opt-out and contribution tracking to 12+ months.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows a high preset default can anchor people at a level worse than they would otherwise choose, and that this bites hardest on lower-income savers, which bears on how aggressively we should pre-select a round-up multiplier and for whom.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
no employer-trust intermediary in our setting
abstract gives opt-out rate but not amounts saved
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly evidences anchoring on a preset default level and heterogeneous harm to lower-income users, both named in the brief's open questions.
alternates.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
alternates.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making. Contributions: conceptualized paper (JB, DL, BM, JC), wrote paper (JB, JC), edited paper (DL), implemented empirical analysis (JB, RG), project leadership (JB, JC). The research reported herein was supported by the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) through grant #10-M-98363-1-02 to the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) as part of the Retirement Research Consortium (RRC). alternates.key_finding: A 2024 overview synthesizes plan-design evidence on automatic enrollment, default investment options, and framing, noting both participation gains and potential negative effects on participant engagement.
alternates.methodology: Narrative overview of defined-contribution plan design literature. Abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a single up-to-date synthesis of the engagement-versus-participation trade-off in the largest analogous literature, useful as a background map even though the mechanism (employer intermediary) does not transfer.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer self-directed product
narrative synthesis, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
alternates.relevance_reason: Broad, recent synthesis of the default/engagement trade-off in the closest analogous literature named by the brief.
alternates.title: Plan Design and Participant Behavior in Defined Contribution Retirement Plans: Past, Present, and Future
alternates.abstract: This paper provides a state-of-the-art overview of defined contribution retirement plan design for academics, policy makers, and industry participants. I begin by considering the impact of basic plan design on participation rates, contribution rates, and portfolio choice, both overall and among employees with lower levels of financial literacy. Next, I consider the short-term and longer-term impacts of automatic enrollment and default investment options, including potential negative effects with respect to participant engagement. I also ask how the framing of plan features and plan communication can impact participant behavior. Finally, I examine recent plan changes including the integration of life annuities into retirement plans and target date funds (TDFs), managed accounts as alternatives to TDFs, emergency savings accounts, state-sponsored retirement plans, and national legislation like SECURE 2.0 that is intended to increase plan access and opportunities for employer matches.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised wealth accumulation substantially while active-choice tax subsidies induced only 1 cent of new saving per dollar of subsidy, because 85% of savers are 'passive' and unresponsive to active incentives.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data analysis, population-level, Denmark.
alternates.why_it_matters: The canonical large-N demonstration that passive/default policies dominate active-choice-based incentives for the majority of savers, but it is the foundational retirement-plan result the brief explicitly says needs updating for a liquid, self-directed consumer app.
limitations: retirement/tax-advantaged accounts, not liquid consumer savings
government/employer intermediary mechanism does not carry to a banking app
does not address active-choice-in-onboarding as a design, only active vs passive saving behavior generally
alternates.relevance_reason: The most-cited large-scale evidence for the default effect the internal argument leans on, useful as the benchmark this project's data should be measured against but capped by domain mismatch.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrollees actively opted back out, and the default effect was strongest when incentives were high and knowledge of enrollment status was low.
alternates.methodology: Natural experiment using nationwide policy rollout, linked administrative and survey data.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows a large default effect size decaying quickly through active opt-out, and ties the effect's strength to complexity/incentive salience and awareness -- relevant to whether our round-up default would similarly erode once users notice they're enrolled.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not a consumer app
low-income employee population may not generalize
alternates.relevance_reason: Large, credible effect-size estimate on default enrollment with explicit heterogeneity by incentive/complexity, close to the brief's C1/C5 questions.
alternates.title: Opt-in or Opt-out? The Power of Defaults in Pension Enrollment Choices
alternates.abstract: Default settings strongly increase pension enrollment, especially when savings incentives are high and choices are complex. We show that the effect is weaker when incentives are low, options are simple, and opting out is easy. We study the nationwide introduction of auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pay-as-you-go pension system. We find that automatic enrollment raises participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opt out. Linking administrative and survey data shows that the default effect is stronger when enrollment incentives are higher and among individuals who lack knowledge of their enrollment status.

alternates.key_finding: Randomizing default enrolment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, equivalent to a 50% match incentive, with the effect attributed largely to present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios rather than employer trust.
alternates.methodology: Field experiment with random assignment to different default savings-account variants among salaried employees in Afghanistan, with follow-up interventions isolating mechanisms.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests why defaults work (present bias, cognitive cost) rather than just that they work, which matters for predicting whether an opt-out round-up default will produce genuine engagement or just passive non-opt-out; also finds defaults increased later active saving, a data point against pure disengagement.
limitations: salary-linked account still routed through an employer paymaster, retaining some intermediary-trust mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
developing-country labor-market setting far from an EU consumer banking app
no 6-12 month withdrawal or amount-saved data reported
alternates.relevance_reason: Offers mechanism-level evidence on why default effects occur, relevant to judging whether the same mechanism would produce engaged versus vanity enrolment in the app.
alternates.title: Why Do Defaults Affect Behavior? Experimental Evidence from Afghanistan
alternates.abstract: We report on an experiment examining why default options impact behavior. By randomly assigning employees to different varieties of a salary-linked savings account, we find that default enrollment increases participation by 40 percentage points—an effect equivalent to providing a 50 percent matching incentive. We then use a series of experimental interventions to differentiate between explanations for the default effect, which we conclude is driven largely by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of thinking through different savings scenarios. Default assignment also changes employees’ attitudes toward saving, and makes them more likely to actively decide to save after the study concludes. (JEL C93, D14, D91, O12)
